problemText: During an eclipse event, the three bodies — Sun, Moon, and Earth — line up close to a straight line. The body that sits in the middle of this line is the one doing the blocking and casting a shadow. If the Moon is the body in the middle, which type of eclipse is happening?
choices: A solar eclipse, because Earth's shadow reaches the Moon
A lunar eclipse, because the Moon's shadow reaches the Moon
A solar eclipse, because the Moon's shadow reaches Earth
A lunar eclipse, because Earth's shadow reaches Earth
hints: Remember: the body in the middle does the blocking.
If the Moon is in the middle, whose shadow can reach where?

problemText: At a certain full moon, Earth, the Sun, and the Moon line up almost exactly in this order: Sun, Earth, Moon. The Moon appears dark as viewed from Earth. What is happening, and why does this event occur at full moon rather than at some other lunar phase?
choices: A solar eclipse is happening because Earth sits between the Sun and Moon at full moon, which is the only time Earth's shadow can reach the Moon
A solar eclipse is happening because the Moon sits between the Sun and Earth only at full moon, when the Moon can block sunlight from reaching Earth
A lunar eclipse is happening because the Moon sits between the Sun and Earth at full moon, allowing Earth's shadow to fall on the Moon
A lunar eclipse is happening because Earth sits between the Sun and Moon only at full moon, when Earth can block sunlight from reaching the Moon
hints: At full moon, which body sits in the middle of the Sun-Earth-Moon line?
Which body does the blocking when Earth is in the middle?

problemText: During a new moon, the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up in that order: Sun, Moon, Earth. As the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, its shadow falls on part of Earth's daytime side. Why does the Moon's shadow only cover a narrow strip of Earth's surface rather than the entire daytime side?
choices: The Moon's shadow is small compared to Earth, so at any moment it only covers a narrow strip as it moves across Earth's daytime side
The Moon is positioned so far from Earth that its shadow spreads out significantly and loses intensity before striking Earth's surface
Earth's atmosphere is thick enough to scatter and disperse the Moon's shadow into many separate narrow bands instead of one continuous shadow
The Moon's orbit tilts at about 5 degrees relative to Earth's orbit, which constrains the shadow to a narrow path along that orbital angle
hints: Compare the size of the Moon to the size of Earth.
When a small object casts a shadow on a much larger object, what shape does that shadow have?

problemText: Earth has a new moon roughly every 14.75 days and a full moon roughly every 14.75 days after that, for a cycle of about 29.5 days. This means there should be a new moon and a full moon about twice per month. However, solar eclipses happen far less often than twice per month, and lunar eclipses also happen much more rarely than twice per month. Using what you know about the Moon's orbit and the conditions for an eclipse to occur, explain why eclipses are so rare even though new and full moons happen regularly.
choices: The Moon's orbital distance varies periodically, which causes its shadow to change size dramatically and miss Earth entirely during most new moon phases

The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees from Earth's orbit around the Sun, so at most new and full moons the Moon sits above or below the straight line needed for an eclipse, and eclipses only happen at the few new and full moons where the orbits cross

Earth's thick atmosphere scatters and absorbs the Moon's shadow during new moons and also blocks Earth's shadow from reaching the Moon during full moons, preventing eclipses from occurring at regular intervals

The Sun's gravitational pull on the Moon changes throughout Earth's orbit, causing the Moon's position to shift away from the eclipse line at most new and full moons, so alignment only happens occasionally
hints: What tilts by 5 degrees, and what two points does this create where actual line-up can occur?
At how many new and full moons does the Moon sit on the exact straight line an eclipse needs?

problemText: Two eclipse events occur in the same calendar year. The first happens at new moon, when the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up as Sun-Moon-Earth. Several months later, at a full moon, the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up as Sun-Earth-Moon. Compare these two events: which one is visible from a wider area of Earth, and why does the difference happen?
choices: The first event is visible from a wider area because the Moon's shadow expands as it travels toward Earth, allowing it to cover a much larger surface area than Earth's shadow ever could

The first event is visible from a wider area because new moons occur more frequently than full moons throughout the year, which gives the Moon's shadow additional chances to intersect with Earth's surface
The second event is visible from a wider area because Earth's shadow is much larger than the Moon's shadow, so the Moon sits fully inside it and is visible from the entire night side of Earth at once

The second event is visible from a wider area because the Moon passes through Earth's shadow during full moon, and the size of Earth's shadow at the Moon's distance is much larger than the Moon itself
hints: In the first event, a small shadow sweeps across a large surface. In the second event, a large shadow covers a small target. Which situation lets more people see it?
How does the size of Earth's shadow compare to the size of the Moon?

problemText: A student reasons as follows: 'New moons happen about every 14.75 days because the Moon orbits Earth about every 29.5 days. If I wait for the next new moon after an eclipse, there should be another solar eclipse about 14.75 days later, because the Sun, Moon, and Earth will line up the same way again.' Evaluate this reasoning. Is the student correct, or is there a flaw in the reasoning? Use what you know about why eclipses actually occur to explain your answer.
choices: The student is correct; if the bodies line up for an eclipse once, they will line up the same way again at the next new moon because the Moon returns to the same orbital position
The student is incorrect; Earth's shadow moves around Earth every 24 hours, which prevents the Moon from reaching the same position in space again for several months until alignment is restored

The student is incorrect; the Moon's orbital period of 27.3 days means the timing between successive new moons does not match the actual time needed for the Moon to return to an eclipse-favorable position

The student is incorrect; although new moons do happen every 14.75 days, eclipses do not occur at every new moon because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees from Earth's orbit, so most new moons have the Moon above or below the straight line needed for an eclipse
hints: Just because the Moon returns to new moon phase does not mean it is in the same position relative to the Sun-Earth plane. What prevents that?
Where are the only places an eclipse can happen, given the Moon's orbital tilt?

problemText: Half of the Moon is always lit by the sun, just as half of Earth is always lit during daytime. What word describes the shape of the lit part of the Moon that we can see from Earth on any given night?
choices: Orbit
Phase
Eclipse
Crescent
hints: The term you are looking for is the general name for any shape the Moon appears to have, not just one specific shape.
This word comes directly from the definition: the shape of the lit part we can see from Earth at a given time.

problemText: A student observes the Moon in the sky and sees a thin sliver of light on the right side, with the rest of the Moon's disk dark. The Moon sets shortly after the sun goes down. Based on the Moon's position in its orbit and the direction of the lit part, which phase is the student observing?
choices: First quarter
Waning crescent
Waxing crescent
Waning gibbous
hints: A thin sliver is a crescent. To decide if it is waxing or waning, think about what will happen to the lit part over the next few nights.
In the Northern Hemisphere, the lit part of a waxing moon appears on the right side of the Moon. A crescent that sets soon after sunset means the Moon is early in its cycle.

problemText: An astronomer notes that the Moon is visible high in the southern sky at sunset and looks like a perfect half circle, with the right half lit and the left half dark. Approximately how far through its cycle from new moon to new moon has the Moon traveled?
choices: All the way back to new moon
One half of the way
Three quarters of the way
One quarter of the way
hints: A half-circle shape is called first or third quarter, depending on whether the lit part is growing or shrinking. The name 'quarter' refers to how far through the orbit, not how much you see.
The lit part is on the right and the Moon is high at sunset, which means it is still growing. A waxing moon that looks like a half circle is at the first quarter point in the cycle.

problemText: A student sketches the Moon's position at three different times over two weeks. In the first sketch, the Moon is between Earth and the sun. In the second sketch (one week later), Earth is between the sun and the Moon. In the third sketch (two weeks after the first), the Moon is between Earth and the sun again. For each position, describe what someone on the night side of Earth would see, and explain why Earth's shadow does not cause the change from the first observation to the second.
choices: First: new moon, almost nothing visible. Second: full moon, entire disk visible. The angle between sun, Moon, and Earth changes as the Moon orbits, not because Earth's shadow moves.
First: full moon, entire disk visible. Second: new moon, almost nothing visible. The angle between sun, Moon, and Earth changes as the Moon orbits, not because Earth's shadow moves.
First: new moon, almost nothing visible. Second: full moon, entire disk visible. Earth's shadow cannot explain the change because the shadow always points away from the sun.
First: full moon, entire disk visible. Second: new moon, almost nothing visible. Earth's shadow cannot explain the change because it only happens during a lunar eclipse.
hints: When the Moon is between Earth and the sun, the lit half faces away from us. When Earth is between the sun and the Moon, the lit half faces toward us.
The reason Earth's shadow is not the cause is that it always points straight away from the sun, so it cannot be reaching the Moon at random times as phases change every week.

problemText: A student sees the Moon in the western sky just after sunset. The lit part is a thin crescent on the right side. Over the next two weeks, the student observes the Moon every few nights and notes that it appears higher and higher in the evening sky, and the lit part grows larger each night, moving from right to left across the Moon's face. At the end of this two-week period, the student looks for the Moon at midnight and finds it high in the southern sky, completely illuminated. Name the phase at the start and the phase at the end, and explain why the lit part appears to move from right side to left side over this time.
choices: Start: waning crescent. End: full moon. The lit part appears to move from right to left because the Moon is orbiting Earth, and from our fixed viewpoint on Earth, we see more and more of the lit hemisphere each night.

Start: waxing crescent. End: full moon. The lit part appears to move from right to left because the Moon is orbiting Earth, and from our fixed viewpoint on Earth, we see more and more of the lit hemisphere each night.
Start: waxing crescent. End: full moon. The lit part appears to move from right to left because the half of the Moon facing the sun rotates around to face us as the cycle progresses.
Start: waxing crescent. End: waning gibbous. The lit part appears to move from right to left because Earth rotates on its axis, causing the Moon to appear to move across the sky.
hints: A thin crescent is a crescent. In the Northern Hemisphere, a crescent with light on the right side means the lit part is growing, not shrinking.
The apparent motion of the lit edge from right to left happens because the angle between the sun, Moon, and Earth keeps changing as the Moon orbits, not because the Moon itself is rotating toward us.

problemText: A student in the Northern Hemisphere observes the Moon at sunset on four different dates spread over six weeks. On Date 1, the Moon is high in the southern sky and completely lit. On Date 2 (about seven days later), the Moon is not visible at sunset or for hours afterward. On Date 3 (about seven days after Date 2), the Moon is visible in the eastern sky before sunrise, still not visible at sunset, and shows a thin crescent on the left side. On Date 4 (about seven days after Date 3), the Moon is low in the eastern sky just before sunrise and shows a half-circle shape with the left side lit. Explain why the Moon is NOT visible at sunset on Date 2, describe the phase on Date 4 using both its name and a reason based on the Sun-Moon-Earth angle, and identify the error in this statement: 'The Moon disappears from the evening sky because Earth's shadow blocks the sunlight from reaching the Moon at new moon.'
choices: Date 2: waning gibbous, not visible because it sets with the sun and is too faint to see. Date 4: first quarter, because the Moon is still moving away from full moon and half of it is lit by the sun. Error: Earth's shadow only blocks light during a lunar eclipse, which happens rarely and is a different event from the normal monthly phases.

Date 2: new moon, not visible because the lit half faces away from Earth and the Moon is positioned near the sun in the sky. Date 4: waning crescent, because the lit part is shrinking as the Moon moves back toward new moon and only a sliver remains lit. Error: Earth's shadow is actually what causes the Moon to disappear, but it only affects the Moon during new moon when the shadow is strongest and most direct.

Date 2: new moon, not visible because the lit half faces away from Earth. Date 4: third quarter, because Earth is no longer between the sun and the Moon, and the angle now shows half the lit side. Error: Earth's shadow does not cause phases; the Moon disappears because of the Sun-Moon-Earth angle, not because of a shadow.

Date 2: new moon, not visible because the lit half faces away from Earth and lies between the sun and Earth in orbit. Date 4: waning gibbous, because the Moon is approaching new moon again and most of its lit side still faces Earth. Error: Earth's shadow does not cause phases; phases happen every month but eclipses are rare events that last only hours when the shadow actually touches the Moon.
hints: Count the phases carefully in order: full moon (Date 1), then new moon (Date 2), then waxing crescent (Date 3 — early morning, left side lit). Trace what comes next.

The key to the error is that Earth's shadow is real but does not cause the regular monthly shape changes we call phases. Phases come from the angle; eclipses from the rare alignment when the shadow actually falls on the Moon.

problemText: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees and stays pointed toward the same direction in space all year long. What is the name of this imaginary line that Earth spins around?
choices: axis
orbit
equator
revolution
hints: This is the line running through Earth's center that it rotates on.
The problem says the axis stays pointed the same way all year.

problemText: Imagine you are standing on Earth at a location in the Northern Hemisphere on a day when Earth's tilt points that hemisphere toward the sun. The sun is high overhead and the day lasts about 15 hours. Based on what causes seasons, which season is it where you are standing?
choices: Winter
Summer
Spring
Autumn
hints: A high, overhead sun and longer daylight hours indicate a hemisphere that is tilted toward the sun.
When a hemisphere is tilted toward the sun, it experiences the season with the warmest, longest days.

problemText: In January, Earth's tilt points the Northern Hemisphere away from the sun. At that same moment, where is the Southern Hemisphere's tilt pointing, and what season is it there?
choices: Away from the sun, and it is summer
Toward the sun, and it is winter
Toward the sun, and it is summer
Away from the sun, and it is winter
hints: Remember that Earth's axis keeps pointing one fixed direction while the planet revolves, so the two hemispheres are always tilted opposite ways.
If the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away in January, the Southern Hemisphere must be tilted the opposite direction.

problemText: A student claims that the Northern Hemisphere has warmer weather in July because Earth is closest to the sun at that time of year. Explain why this claim is wrong using two pieces of evidence: one about Earth's actual orbit, and one about what happens in the Southern Hemisphere at the same moment.
choices: Earth is actually farthest from the sun in July, and the Southern Hemisphere is also warm in July, so the cause cannot be distance.
Earth is actually farthest from the sun in July, but we cannot know what the Southern Hemisphere experiences without more information.
Earth is actually nearest to the sun in July, but the Southern Hemisphere is having winter, which proves distance does not control seasons.
Earth is actually farthest from the sun in July, and the Southern Hemisphere is having winter at that same moment, so the cause cannot be distance.
hints: Check whether the orbit fact and the hemisphere fact together rule out distance as the cause.
If distance were the cause, both hemispheres on the same planet at the same distance would have to share the same season.

problemText: At a certain moment in Earth's orbit, the sunlight arriving at a location in Australia (Southern Hemisphere) hits at a steep angle close to overhead, and that location experiences about 14 hours of daylight. Earth's axis is still tilted the same fixed way it always is. What is happening at that same moment in the Arctic region of the Northern Hemisphere, and why?
choices: The Arctic is receiving slanted, low-angle sunlight and has about 10 hours of daylight because the tilted axis points the Southern Hemisphere toward the sun and the Northern Hemisphere away.
The Arctic is receiving steep overhead sunlight and has about 14 hours of daylight due to both hemispheres being positioned at similar distances from the sun at this moment in the orbit.

The Arctic is receiving steep overhead sunlight and has about 14 hours of daylight because at any given moment in Earth's orbit, the tilted axis causes both hemispheres to lean toward the sun equally.

The Arctic is receiving no sunlight and has zero hours of daylight because Earth's position in its orbit places the entire Northern Hemisphere in permanent darkness while the Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the sun.
hints: If Australia has the tilted-toward-the-sun conditions, what opposite conditions must the Arctic have from the tilted-away-from-the-sun hemisphere?
The tilted axis always points one fixed way, so when one hemisphere faces the sun directly, the other hemisphere faces away.

problemText: During a full year, Earth completes one revolution around the sun while its tilted axis always points the same direction in space. At four key points in this orbit—near January, April, July, and October—a student observes the angle and intensity of sunlight at a fixed location in the Northern Hemisphere and notes the day length. Near January, the sun is low and weak, and day length is short. Near July, the sun is high and strong, and day length is long. Based on the fixed-tilt-plus-revolution model, explain why the Northern Hemisphere sees exactly this pattern twice per year (once going toward summer and once coming away from it), and identify what remains constant throughout the entire year that makes this repetition possible.
choices: The tilt angle and sun distance change throughout the year, creating the pattern twice by coincidence, because the orbit causes Earth to pass through regions of varying solar intensity at regular intervals during each revolution.

The hemisphere's tilt relative to the sun's direction changes from pointing away to pointing toward and back again as Earth revolves, while the axis itself always points the same fixed direction in space, causing the regular back-and-forth pattern.

The sun's brightness relative to the Northern Hemisphere increases as the tilt rotates to aim toward the sun, then decreases as the tilt rotates away, and this cycle repeats twice per year because the axis always points the same fixed direction while Earth orbits.

The length of Earth's axis changes slightly during the year in response to gravitational forces, making the tilt angle alternate between pointing toward and away from the sun twice per complete revolution around the sun.
hints: What one thing about Earth's axis never changes no matter where Earth is in its orbit, and how does that fixed thing create a back-and-forth pattern as Earth travels around the sun?
In six months, Earth moves to the opposite side of its orbit—the axis still points the same way, so the Northern Hemisphere's tilt relative to the sun flips completely.

problemText: Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours, completing a full spin around an imaginary line running through the North and South Poles. What is the name for this spinning motion?
choices: Tilt
Revolution
Orbit
Rotation
hints: This motion is a complete spin around an imaginary line running through the North and South Poles.
This motion takes about 24 hours and is different from the year-long trip around the sun.

problemText: At this very moment, sunlight is lighting exactly one half of Earth while the other half is in darkness. A person standing in the dark half is currently experiencing nighttime. What will happen to that person's location as Earth continues to spin?
choices: It will be carried by Earth's rotation into the lit half, where daytime will arrive.
It will stay in darkness permanently because darkness does not move.
It will move toward the sun, which will eventually reach the horizon and rise.
It will experience sunset as the sun moves away to the other side of the planet.
hints: Think about what happens to a location when Earth's spin carries it from one side of the planet to the other.
The lit half and the dark half do not stay in the same place — they stay connected to the sunlight and space, while Earth rotates underneath them.

problemText: Earth spins from west to east, which means if you looked down at the North Pole from high above, the spin would appear counterclockwise. From the ground, a person standing in most of the Northern Hemisphere sees the sun rise somewhere in the east and set somewhere in the west. Which statement correctly explains why the sun appears to move this way across the sky?
choices: The sun orbits Earth once per day, traveling from east to west, which makes it visible in the eastern sky at sunrise.
Earth's spin carries the ground toward the east, so the sun appears to move the opposite way, from east to west, even though the sun itself has not moved.
The tilt of Earth's axis points the Northern Hemisphere toward the sun during the day and away at night, making the sun appear to cross the sky.
The sun moves around Earth from west to east, but the spin of the planet makes it look like the sun is moving the other direction.
hints: Think of spinning in a desk chair — the room appears to turn around you, but the room has not actually moved.
The sun itself is not moving around Earth; the apparent motion belongs to Earth's rotation.

problemText: Two locations sit on Earth along lines of longitude that are 45 degrees apart, with Location X to the west and Location Y to the east. Earth rotates from west to east at a rate of 15 degrees per hour (360 degrees divided by 24 hours). Based on this rotation rate and direction, how many hours apart do the sunrises occur at these two locations, and which location experiences sunrise first?
choices: Location X experiences sunrise 3 hours first because it is farther west.
Location X experiences sunrise 15 hours first because it takes 15 degrees per hour to rotate.
Location Y experiences sunrise 3 hours first because it is farther east and Earth spins toward the east.
Both locations experience sunrise at the same time because they are only 45 degrees apart.
hints: Divide the longitude distance (45 degrees) by the rotation rate (15 degrees per hour) to find the time gap.
Remember that because Earth spins west to east, the eastern location crosses the sunrise line before the western location does.

problemText: A student observes that the sun appears to move across the sky at a steady rate throughout the day, taking roughly the same amount of time to go from sunrise to midday as it takes to go from midday to sunset. Another student says this steady apparent motion proves that the sun is moving around Earth at a constant speed. Evaluate this reasoning using the rotation model, and explain what the steady rate actually tells us about Earth.
choices: The reasoning is correct because the sun's steady motion across the sky can only happen if the sun is orbiting Earth at a constant rate.
The reasoning is incorrect because the rotation model does not explain the sun's motion; it only explains why day and night happen.
The reasoning is partially correct for the hours around midday but incorrect for sunrise and sunset, when the sun moves faster because it is lower in the sky.

The reasoning is incorrect. The steady apparent motion of the sun reflects Earth's steady rotation rate, not the sun's motion. The fact that the sun appears to move at a consistent rate tells us that Earth is spinning at a constant rate.
hints: What is actually turning at a steady rate — the sun or Earth?
If Earth's spin rate did not change, what would that predict about how the sun appears to move across the sky?

problemText: A location on Earth is currently at sunrise — the sun is just appearing on the horizon. Earth's rotation carries all points at 15 degrees per hour. The tilt of Earth's axis does not change the rotation rate or the fact that exactly half of Earth is lit at any moment. Given that the location is currently at sunrise, approximately how many more hours will pass before the sun reaches its highest point in the sky at that location?
choices: Exactly 6 hours, because the location must rotate 90 degrees from sunrise to reach the highest point, and 90 degrees divided by 15 degrees per hour equals 6 hours.
Exactly 12 hours, because the sun must complete half of its apparent journey across the sky.
Between 5 and 7 hours, because Earth's tilt affects how high the sun climbs and how quickly it moves across the sky.
It is impossible to calculate without knowing the latitude of the location and the time of year, because the tilt changes everything about the sun's path.
hints: The tilt does not change how long one rotation takes — the rotation rate stays at 15 degrees per hour all year.
From sunrise to highest point in the sky is a quarter turn of the Earth — calculate how many degrees that is, then use the rotation rate to find the time.
